problem: Online topological VLN-CE planners (ETPNav-style) encode ghost-node candidates from raw 2D depth views that contain distant, irrelevant geometry, and as the graph grows historical nodes dilute the planner's attention on the current frontier candidates.
motivation: The agent's immediate motion range is bounded (about 3 m), so far-range depth is weakly related to the next waypoint decision. Truncating in the 2D image domain breaks depth continuity and hurts the visual backbone. Enhancement that accumulates over the global graph interferes with local decisions at intersections.
key_idea: Project each ghost node's depth view to a 3D point cloud, truncate it along Z at 3 m, encode it with PointNet, and residually add it to only the current ghost nodes' features, discarding it once they become visited or obsolete.
insight: Truncation must happen in 3D: 2D cropping drops SR from 63.24 to 51.82 (global) and 58.08 (local) for ETP-R1 SFT, while 3D truncation helps. Local-only enhancement with degradation beats global enhancement (SFT SPL 55.21 vs 54.69; SR 63.89 vs 63.13). A learnable-scalar weighted fusion beats direct addition, which falls below the baseline. A 3 m truncation beats none or 5 m (SR 65.13 vs 61.50 and 64.43), and 256 points is as good as 1024 but faster.
method: 3D lifting: back-project each ghost node's candidate depth view to a dense point cloud using camera intrinsics
Depth-directed hard truncation: keep points with z<=3.0 m (aligned with the waypoint range), cropping along the camera Z-axis rather than a spherical cutoff
FPS downsampling: farthest point sampling to a fixed 256 points
PointNet encoder: shared MLP [64,128,256] with BatchNorm, no dropout, max-pool to a global feature g_j in R^D
Dimension-preserving residual fusion: v_enh = v_ghost + lambda * (W_proj g_j), with a learnable scalar lambda and bypass projection W_proj, leaving token dimensions and planner interface unchanged
Transient state degradation: geometric vectors are applied only to ghost nodes linked to the current node, and are discarded when a node is selected or becomes an obsolete frontier
Parameter-efficient training: the baseline is frozen and only PointNet, W_proj and lambda are trained for at most 1000 iterations (about 3 h on 2x RTX 4090)

setting.backbone: Frozen pre-trained topological planner (ETPNav / BEVBert / DGNav / ETP-R1 SFT or RFT) plus a trained lightweight PointNet, projection and scalar
setting.training_data: R2R-CE and RxR-CE training data used to tune only the new modules for at most 1000 iterations; no extra data
setting.action_space: ghost-node waypoints in the topological graph, executed by a low-level controller (MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN 15°, STOP)

numbers.extra: Only the LCG parameters were tuned, for at most 1000 iterations. Table 1 prints OSR/SR/SPL as integers; Table 2 gives the decimals.
numbers.evidence: Table 2 LCG-R1(RFT); Table 1 prints LCG-ETP-R1 as NE 3.93, OSR 71, SR 65, SPL 57

numbers_note: Table 1 prints OSR/SR/SPL as integers for LCG-ETP-R1 (71/65/57). Decimals come from Table 2. The RxR-CE comparison against other methods appears only in Table 2.
results: LCG-ETP-R1 (RFT) reaches NE 3.93, SR 65.14 and SPL 56.85 on R2R-CE val-unseen. In Table 1 it beats WP-CMA (NE 4.52, SR 59) and JanusVLN (NE 4.78). Attached to five baselines, LCGNav improves most metrics on R2R-CE and every reported metric on RxR-CE, but the gains are small (about 0.5-1 SR points). It slightly lowers SR/OSR for ETP-R1 (RFT) and BEVBert on R2R-CE.
limitations: The gains over baselines are small, and some R2R-CE metrics get worse (e.g. OSR and SR for RFT, NE for BEVBert)
It relies on clean simulator depth and camera intrinsics; sensor noise and real-robot deployment are untested
It requires a pre-trained topological baseline and is only evaluated in Habitat/MP3D; Table 1 also mixes end-to-end and map-based methods with differing training regimes
